title: The Centre-state divide in food safety regulation
syllabus: GS2 › Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; issues in the federal structure · GS2 › Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies · GS2 › Issues relating to health · GS4 › Good governance
summary: Maharashtra has gone to the Bombay High Court alleging that the national regulator FSSAI created a parallel enforcement mechanism and encroached on the state's powers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
ideas: Act gives enforcement to states; FSSAI sets standards and licenses big firms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
National standards, local enforcement.
FSSAI's central inspectors and wider licensing seen as a parallel mechanism.
GS2 · Federal friction
Regulators can redraw federalism by executive order.
Rules changed without public consultation weaken legitimacy.
GS2 · Rule of law / GS4 · Transparency
Process matters as much as purpose.
keywords: A central body duplicating enforcement that a law gives to states
A parallel regulatory mechanism breeds turf wars and confuses businesses about whom to answer to.
Rules and orders made by an executive body under powers given by a statute
Delegated legislation must stay within the parent Act; orders creating central FSOs test that limit.
How regulatory powers are shared between national and state authorities
Food safety is a test of regulatory federalism: national standards, local enforcement.
Outcomes that rest on one officer's leadership rather than systems
A central official asked whether Maharashtra's good enforcement would survive one officer's transfer: institutions must outlast individuals.
examples: GST Council: Centre and states decide together.
FSSAI and states acting on one food safety scare
Maggi ban, 2015: FSSAI and states acting on one food safety scare.
Pre-legislative consultation: public comment before rules.
pyqs: Recent changes in Centre-State relations; building trust.
National parties' centralisation vs regional parties' autonomy.
CBI jurisdiction in states; withholding consent.
CCI curbing abuse of dominance by MNCs.
State's role in containing marketisation of public healthcare.

trend.t: Centre–state questions have moved from constitutional devices (Article 356, 2023; Governors, 2022 and 2026) to everyday friction in shared domains: CBI consent (2021), building trust (2024) and fiscal federalism (2025). Regulatory bodies are asked one at a time (CCI 2023, tribunals 2025).
trend.watch: Centre–state relations have been asked every year from 2021 to 2026, increasingly through concrete disputes, so a regulator–state turf war like FSSAI is the kind of example UPSC now rewards.
focus: Concurrent-list domains: health, food, police cooperation
Delegated legislation and limits of regulators

potential: "Regulatory bodies are becoming a new site of Centre–state friction." Examine with reference to food safety regulation in India. (10 marks)
Discuss how cooperative federalism can be strengthened in regulatory domains shared by the Union and the States. (15 marks)

practice.q: "Regulatory bodies are becoming a new site of Centre–state friction." Examine with reference to food safety regulation in India.
parts: The case for a central role

answer.t: In 2026 Maharashtra moved the Bombay High Court alleging that FSSAI had built a 'parallel enforcement mechanism' that encroaches on state powers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

pts.t: Regulators expand roles through orders rather than amendments.
pts.ex: FSSAI's May 2023 order creating central FSOs, though the Act vests appointment in state Commissioners.

pts.t: Central licensing widened to new categories.
pts.ex: E-commerce platforms, five-star hotels, nutraceuticals and proprietary foods.

pts.t: Rules changed without consultation erode trust.
pts.ex: March 2026 threshold change from Rs 20 crore to Rs 50 crore without public consultation.

pts.t: States inspect but must report to the central authority, which runs proceedings.
pts.ex: Reports from state officers go to the central licensing authority.

answer.h: The case for a central role

pts.t: Enforcement varies across states and over time.
pts.ex: A central official's concern that one state's record depends on one officer.

pts.t: Inter-state and export businesses need one standard.
pts.ex: Central licence for businesses operating across state lines.

pts.t: If central enforcement is needed, Parliament should amend the Act.
Shared inspection protocols and data between FSSAI and state commissioners.
pts.ex: A food safety council on the GST Council model.

pts.t: Mandatory public and state consultation before rule changes.

answer.t: Food safety needs one standard and many hands: national rules enforced locally, with states treated as partners, not subordinates.

title: With decline in poverty, shift focus — from free food to nutritional security
where: Ideas page, page 9 (Ashok Gulati, Ritika Juneja and Sulakshana Rao, ICRIER)
syllabus: GS3 › Food security; public distribution system; buffer stocks · GS3 › Agriculture: soil health, biofortification · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty and hunger; malnutrition
summary: Using the World Bank brief, the authors argue that with extreme poverty at 2.6%, free grain to 81 crore people under PM-GKY should be rationalised and reoriented to nutrition: food coupons, biofortified staples and healthier soils.
ideas: Poverty fell faster after 2004: growth up, population growth down.
GS3 · Growth and poverty
Fewer mouths share each rupee of growth.
Farm growth cuts poverty 2.5x more (World Development Report 2008).
GS3 · Agriculture
Invest in farms to cut poverty.
Free grain to ~81 crore needs rationalising at 2.6% extreme poverty.
GS3 · Food subsidies
Target the poorest, price the rest.
From calories to nutrition: coupons, biofortified staples, healthier soils.
GS3 · Nutrition security
Nutrition starts in the soil.
keywords: Access to a diet with adequate nutrients, not just calories
India has achieved food security; nutrition security is the next goal.
Carbon in soil that sustains fertility and nutrient uptake
India's SOC of about 0.3% against a desirable 1.5–2% explains nutrient-poor grain.
Breeding crops richer in micronutrients like iron and zinc
Biofortified wheat and rice can fight hidden hunger through the PDS.
Free wheat and rice fill stomachs but not the gap of hidden hunger.
data: India's soil organic carbon against the desirable level
World Food Laureate Rattan Lal (cited by the authors)
GS3 · Soil health
India's soil organic carbon is around 0.3%, against a desirable 1.5–2%, says Rattan Lal.
≥2.5 times
How much more potent agricultural growth is in reducing poverty than other growth
World Development Report 2008 (42 countries, 1981–2003)
GS3 · Agriculture and poverty
The WDR 2008 found farm growth at least 2.5 times more effective at cutting poverty.
examples: iron and zinc through the PDS
Biofortified wheat and rice: iron and zinc through the PDS.
'Teach to fish': empower, don't create dependence.
pyqs: Malnutrition as challenge of social equity, human development, welfare governance.
Breaking the vicious cycle of poverty and malnutrition for human capital.
Millets for health and nutritional security.

trend.t: Food questions moved from distribution (PDS reforms, 2019 and 2022; NFSA, 2021) to nutrition (millets, 2024; poverty–malnutrition cycle, 2024) and in 2026 malnutrition as a challenge of equity and welfare governance.
trend.watch: Malnutrition was asked in 2024 and 2026, and PDS in 2019 and 2022, so the shift 'from food security to nutrition security' is a must-study theme.
focus: Nutrition: millets, pulses, milk and eggs

potential: "India has moved from food scarcity to food security; it must now move to nutrition security." Discuss. (15 marks)
Examine the case for rationalising free food grain under PM-GKY. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India has moved from food scarcity to food security; it must now move to nutrition security." Discuss.

answer.t: The World Bank's October 2026 brief shows India's extreme poverty fell to 2.6% in 2023, yet child malnutrition remains high, so the challenge has moved from calories to nutrients.

pts.t: The National Food Security Act, 2013 made food a right.
Free grain to about 81 crore people.
pts.ex: PM-GKY extended for five years from 2024.

pts.t: Allocations were enhanced to 10 kg per person per month during Covid.
Transfers contributed to falling poverty.
PDS gives wheat and rice, not diverse diets.
pts.ex: Millets, pulses, milk and eggs largely outside PDS.

pts.t: Wheat and rice are deficient in iron and zinc.
Low soil organic carbon reduces nutrient content.
Under-five malnutrition remains very high.
Free grain for over half the population costs heavily.
Flat real farm wages limit diet diversity.
pts.ex: World Bank brief on real earnings.

pts.t: Free for the poorest, part-price for others.
Let families buy healthier foods from designated stores.
Iron- and zinc-rich wheat and rice in the PDS.
Raise soil organic carbon through organic matter and crop diversity.
Shift incentives from rice and wheat to pulses and millets.
Link PDS with Poshan, ICDS and school meals.

answer.t: Viksit Bharat cannot be built on full stomachs and empty plates of nutrients; nutrition security must start in the soil and end on the child's plate.

title: A bullet fired, night call: How 13-member team from India saved a life in Mauritius
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Divya A)
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood (Indian Ocean); India's bilateral relations (Mauritius) · GS4 › Ethics in international relations; compassion
summary: After a young woman was shot near Port Louis amid unrest, Mauritius's Health Minister called India's High Commissioner at night, and a 13-member team from KIMS Hyderabad flew in to operate alongside local doctors; she is recovering.
evolution: Indian Navy rescues the Iranian crew of the Azini, calling India the IOR's 'first responder' (first-responder thread).
ideas: First responder in a crisis: a call from Mauritius's Health Minister to the Indian High Commissioner on the night of October 10 led to a team reaching Mauritius by October 12.
GS2 · India–Mauritius / Indian Ocean
India's overnight medical mission to Mauritius shows the 'first responder' role extending from the sea to hospitals.
Working with, not instead of: doctors judged evacuation to India too risky, so the Indian team operated alongside local doctors; coordination with Mauritian doctors played a major role.
GS2 · Development partnership
Treating the patient in Mauritius with local doctors shows partnership that builds trust and capacity.

Help at a sensitive moment: the shooting, allegedly by a police officer, triggered the most serious unrest in decades; India's help came as the government struggled to restore order and save the patient.
GS2 · Soft power / GS4 · Compassion
Timely humanitarian help during a neighbour's crisis earns goodwill that no treaty can buy.
keywords: Using medical help and health cooperation to build relations
The Mauritius mission is health diplomacy at its most human: one life, two countries.
The country that reaches first when a neighbour faces a crisis
Speed is what makes India a first responder: the team flew within two days of the call.
examples: A 13-member team from KIMS Hyderabad saves a gunshot victim with local doctors
GS2 · India–Mauritius · Soft power · GS4 · Compassion
India's medical mission to Mauritius is an example of compassion serving as diplomacy in the Indian Ocean.
pyqs: Role of ethics and values in human capital, soft power and social harmony.
Soft power such as sports and culture to build goodwill between India and Pakistan.

trend.t: Soft power appears in GS2 (2015, India–Pakistan) and GS4 (2020, comprehensive national power); maritime and Indian Ocean questions have grown (2022–2026).
trend.watch: Indian Ocean partnerships recur in recent GS2 papers; humanitarian help is a useful example for both GS2 and GS4.
focus: India as first responder in the IOR

potential: "Humanitarian assistance has become a pillar of India's Indian Ocean diplomacy." Discuss with examples. (10 marks)

title: More young women adopting menstrual hygiene
where: Your Health, page 12 (Policy Matters: Pally Kundu & Reena Singh, MoHFW)
syllabus: GS2 › Health; Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections and their performance · GS1 › Role of women; Social empowerment · GS4 › Dignity and compassion
summary: NFHS-6 shows 79.2% of women aged 15–24 use hygienic menstrual protection, up from 57.6% in 2015-16, the result of a multi-pronged government strategy.
ideas: A quiet social revolution: hygienic menstrual protection among women aged 15–24 has risen by about 22 percentage points since NFHS-4, so most young women have now moved off cloth and unsafe materials.
GS1 · Women / GS2 · Health
The rise in menstrual hygiene is an underrated marker of women's empowerment and public health progress.

Dignity is part of the definition: WHO–UNICEF define menstrual hygiene as clean material, changed in privacy, safely disposed of, without embarrassment or restriction, linking it to the SDGs on health and gender equality.
GS2 · Health / GS4 · Dignity
Menstrual hygiene is about dignity and freedom from restriction, not just products.

Multi-pronged delivery: the Scheme for Promotion of Menstrual Hygiene under the National Health Mission combines awareness for adolescent girls, subsidised napkins through ASHAs via schools and communities, and safe disposal.
GS2 · Welfare scheme design
Combining awareness, access and disposal through ASHAs and schools shows convergent scheme design.
Affordability through Jan Aushadhi: Suvidha sanitary pads at ₹1 each are distributed through Jan Aushadhi Kendras nationwide.
GS2 · Health access / Affordability
Pricing essential hygiene products at ₹1 removes cost as a barrier for poor households.
Beyond numbers: even small gains mean lakhs of young women switching to safe methods, part of a wider shift in how young women learn, decide and are heard.
GS1 · Social empowerment
Health gains among young women reinforce their education, agency and voice.
keywords: WHO–UNICEF standard of safe, private, dignified menstrual care
India tracks menstrual hygiene management against the WHO–UNICEF benchmark.
Several schemes and institutions working together
Menstrual hygiene gains show convergence of health, education and community platforms.
Services reaching households through ASHAs and schools
ASHAs show frontline delivery is the backbone of health outcomes.
data: Women aged 15–24 using hygienic menstrual protection; 77.6% in NFHS-5 (2019-21), 57.6% in NFHS-4 (2015-16)
NFHS-6, via IE
GS2 · Health / GS1 · Women
79.2% of young women now use hygienic menstrual protection, up from 57.6% in 2015-16 (NFHS-6).
100 crore+ / ₹1
Jan Aushadhi Suvidha sanitary pads sold by January 2026, priced at ₹1 per pad
PMBJP (Jan Aushadhi), via MoHFW officials in IE
GS2 · Health access
Over 100 crore Suvidha pads at ₹1 each have been sold through Jan Aushadhi Kendras.
examples: Affordable pads through 18,000+ Jan Aushadhi Kendras
GS2 · Health access, welfare delivery · GS1 · Women · GS4 · Compassion in public service
₹1 Suvidha pads show how pricing a basic need affordably can change women's health outcomes at scale.
ASHAs and schools as delivery platforms
Subsidised napkins and awareness for adolescent girls
GS2 · Health, community-level delivery · GS1 · Women
ASHAs and schools delivering menstrual hygiene show the power of community-level health interventions.
pyqs: Community-level health interventions for 'Health for All'.
Water, sanitation and hygiene: targeting beneficiaries to outcomes.
Primary health as a moral imperative and a precondition for development.
potential: "Menstrual hygiene is a question of dignity as much as health." Examine India's progress and the remaining challenges. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Menstrual hygiene is a question of dignity as much as health." Examine India's progress and the remaining challenges.

answer.t: NFHS-6 shows 79.2% of women aged 15–24 use hygienic menstrual protection, up from 57.6% in 2015-16.

pts.t: Scheme for Promotion of Menstrual Hygiene under NHM.
ASHAs supply subsidised napkins via schools and communities.
Jan Aushadhi Suvidha pads at ₹1; over 100 crore sold.
Information and education campaigns for adolescent girls.
India tracks the WHO–UNICEF definition.
Social taboos persist beyond product use.
Waste and environmental concerns.
Remote and poor households lag.
Private, clean toilets and water.
Incinerators and biodegradable products.
Break taboos through schools.
Toilets, water and privacy.

answer.t: India has moved young women from cloth to care; the next step is a life free of stigma and restriction.

title: 'I didn't sit on my sofa for a year': The cost of living with OCD
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to health (mental health) · GS4 › Empathy; Attitude and stigma
summary: Minor topic: personal accounts show how shame, misdiagnosis and late treatment turn obsessive-compulsive disorder into years of distress.
ideas: More than neatness: OCD is a mental health condition where intrusive thoughts trigger anxiety and repetitive rituals that bring only brief relief.
GS2 · Mental health
Popular misuse of 'OCD' trivialises a disabling mental illness.
The treatment gap: shame, misdiagnosis and confusion with religious practice delay care; most people live with symptoms for long before their first session.
GS2 · Health access
Stigma and low awareness widen India's mental-health treatment gap.
Treatable with the right care: medication with exposure and response prevention therapy is the standard; psychoeducation for families matters; advanced options such as deep TMS are free at AIIMS.
GS2 · Health services
Combining medication, therapy and family education makes OCD manageable.
keywords: Share of people with a condition who get no care
Delayed diagnosis widens the mental-health treatment gap.
Teaching patients and families about the condition
Psychoeducation reduces stigma and improves treatment success.
data: Prevalence of OCD among Indian adults
National Mental Health Survey (2015-16), via IE
GS2 · Mental health
The National Mental Health Survey estimated OCD prevalence among Indian adults at 0.8%.
examples: Young people hiding symptoms for years before diagnosis
GS2 · Mental health · GS4 · Empathy, attitude and stigma
OCD accounts show that empathy and awareness, not just medicines, decide whether people seek help.
